Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greek Foreign Minister

Athens, Greece

Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis at a Joint Press Availability

Remarks

October 7, 2026

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  (In Greek.) 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.  Thank you for your welcome.  It’s actually great to be here to have our sixth Strategic Dialogue, which is ongoing, and we’ve begun downstairs a few minutes ago.  It’s an event where our two countries commit to continue to work together on a range of issues. 

We are two countries that are bound by a common heritage and by proud histories.  The United States and Greece share a long history of friendship and partnership and alliance.  In fact, the importance of this historical alliance is highlighted by the instability in the world today that we see as a result of conflicts in Hormuz with Iran, or the conflicts in the Red Sea with – in Yemen, or the conflicts in Ukraine and Russia.  As you see a world that faces these destabilizing events, you recognize how important this alliance with Greece is to the United States. 

It’s both historic – historical in its foundation, but it is also critical.  It is a source of stability in an unstable world.  And I’m thankful – we’re thankful – that Greece remains a great ally and that we share a common understanding – this is really important – not just a great ally – we share a common understanding of the threats that face our countries, the face – the threat – that face our societies.  And we share a common understanding about the means to address them. 

One thing we agree on, for example, is that the nations of Europe need to take on a greater share of the burden in defending their continent, and Greece is doing just that.  They’re on track to meet the commitments that have been made to spend 5 percent of their GDP on defense this year, with over 3.5 of that – of their GDP – percent of GDP being spent on core defense.  They’re also joining the National Guard’s Bureau of State Partnership Program, and they’ll be paired, ironically enough, with the Florida National Guard, which will bring our military collaboration even closer. 

Greece is also very close strategic partner on border security in the fight against mass migration, against fighting – they’re a great ally as well on fighting transnational criminal organizations, on counterterrorism.  Due to its geography in the Mediterranean at the crossroads of many of these transit routes, Greece is particularly exposed to the threats posed by mass migration, by human trafficking, by different forms of terror. 

Now, as part of our efforts to combat these common threats to our nations, we’re proud to announce a new Memorandum of Understanding establishing a joint security program to strengthen the counterterrorism information sharing between our respective law enforcement agencies.  What we do not wish to see under any circumstances is that the birthplace of the West is threatened by bad decisions, by inactions, by failure to address challenges.  And so, this program is going to create stronger, more proactive law enforcement cooperation that could readily stop these threats. 

All of these initiatives and more show that Greece is a true and strong and model NATO Ally, a country that understands the importance of burden sharing and is willing to work with partners to address critical threats to all member-states.  Beyond the scope of military operations – because that is not the only part of our relationship that is important – Greece is an important partner in securing the Alliance’s economic future as well.  It plays a vital role in global commerce in a variety of ways and in a variety of industries. 

For example, we share a mutual intent to deepen our collaboration on emerging technology, and we intend to expand U.S. LNG imports and building new gas and electricity interconnectors that strengthen regional energy security and our respective bilateral energy infrastructure. 

And finally, we’re working together to combat antiquities trafficking into the United States, which finances criminal organizations and harms the U.S. art market.  This is an important issue for both of our countries, as we in the U.S. value the artifacts of our Western ancestors just as much as the modern Greeks do.  The State Department, along with our partners in the – in Homeland Security, the FBI, the CBP are cooperating with Greek law enforcement to safeguard cultural property across the Mediterranean to protect our shared cultural heritage from illicit trafficking networks. 

So, today’s Strategic Dialogue, I hope, reflects the strong relationship between our two countries and the breadth of the issues that we’re working together to address.  And I’m grateful for the opportunity to spend time with you and with your colleagues, and I look forward to working with all of you in the future to secure our nations and protect our core interests.  Thank you. 

MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) (Inaudible) Secretary of State.  I will now take a couple of questions.  Please state your name, the media outlet you represent, and to whom you’re directing your question.  (Inaudible) Nikos Meletis (inaudible). 

QUESTION:  (Via interpreter) My question is for Secretary Rubio.  Mr. Secretary, (inaudible) of Europe (inaudible) and the differentiation of energy sources that it is a strategic choice of a U.S. administration.  I wanted to ask to what extent can Greece rely on the support of the U.S. on major projects, initiatives it undertakes in this direction?  It’s not only the Vertical Corridor.  It’s also the ExxonMobil operations, the (inaudible) relations out of Crete, big interconnection (inaudible) interconnection projects of Greece and Egypt, and the other major projects (inaudible) developed a connection between Greece, Cyprus, and Israel.  Thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I can tell you we’re very committed – I guess the other people in the room don’t know what you asked.  Oh, yeah, they do because they’re hearing it on the little radio thing, okay.  I was about to tell you what he asked me, but you know.  So, look, very committed to this.  In addition to the security cooperation, I would argue that energy security is tied to national security.  And if you don’t believe it, just see what’s happening now world with what Iran is trying to do and failing to do, but trying to do. 

So, I think what we have learned is – I think we’ve always known this, but I think recent events reminds us of how it is important to have diverse corridors for energy supply.  We can never be in a situation where, if energy is cut off or energy flows are cut off from one part of the world, the whole world is threatened and the ability of nation-states to act in their best interest is compromised by the leverage that one country or a rogue regime could have over them. 

So, we’re very committed to all of these corridors and to all of these efforts, and Greece is a great partner to do it with.  Obviously, some of the issues you’ve highlighted, some of the things you asked about are tied up and it’s a very delicate situation involving other countries – I won’t say who, but other countries that are involved in some of the things that are complicating that.  And I would just say that issues of that nature that are that delicate and are that critical are probably best addressed through private diplomacy outside the realm of press conferences. 

So let me just leave you with this.  We are very committed to the success of these projects, and we’re very committed to the partnership we have with Greece on energy security, because it’s in Greece’s national interest but it’s also on ours and, I think, is furthering the cause of global security.  And on those issues that you raised, I acknowledge they involve some very sensitive and delicate topics, and we intend to address them in proper forum so they can be addressed. 

I know – we like to be transparent, but there are things in global affairs that are best not debated at press conferences but handled at the table of dialogue.  And by the way, I want to commend your foreign minister for always being someone who’s been out there working very hard to seek dialogue and stability in the world.  He’s committed a lot to it personally, and it’s something we appreciate and acknowledge.

MODERATOR:  Thank you.  (Inaudible) next question.  Yes, I believe in the center, Ms. Gazis. 

QUESTION:  Thank you very much.  Olivia Gazis with CBS News.  Two questions for you, Mr. Secretary. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  See, they always cheat.  My American people – your guy asked one question, and they always ask two – they get one, but they get two.  Go ahead.

QUESTION:  There’s a lot of news around —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  They’re always cheating.  We gotta do a rule here.  Go ahead. 

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  Maximalists. 

QUESTION:  I know you are both well versed in fielding press inquiries.  (Laughter.) 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, sometimes it’s three – it’s not even two, it’s three.  So, she’s being reasonable.  Go ahead. 

QUESTION:  Thank you very much.  Mr. Secretary, yesterday the Vice President said that Iran needed to do something meaningful to its nuclear enrichment capacity.  Is that to say that the U.S. is now open to an enrichment capacity above zero in Iran?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t think it means that —

QUESTION:  This is my second question, if you don’t mind. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay. 

QUESTION:  If I may, amid increasing congressional scrutiny of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s tenure here, I’m wondering, Mr. Secretary, if you’ve personally reviewed some of those allegations and are confident that all is in compliance with State Department ethics.  If you’d like to answer, then I can pose the question to the minister.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Pose what question to the minister?

QUESTION:  I’ll just do the third question to the minister, that is – so the only question to the minister.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, she’s got three questions – I told you.  Well, I’m —

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  (Inaudible.)  (Laughter.) 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, look, on the second question, this is not the forum where we’re going to address that, as simple as that.  Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job.  Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.  The questions you’re asking me, we’re not addressing those at press conferences in Greece with the foreign minister and in another country. 

That said, on your first question, look, it’s very – I don’t understand what the confusion is about the nuclear program.  Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, simple, period, and end of story.  I’m not going to go into the details about what would be acceptable or not.  I can tell you this, that they’re not going to ever have a nuclear program.  And anything they agree to that would be acceptable to the United States has to be something that ensures that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.  That is what our position is; that is the reason why this began. 

And it’s important to understand – and I’ve raised this multiple times; I’ll raise it again – what Iran was trying to do was build up a conventional capability so massive that they would become untouchable.  In essence, they would come to the world in a year or two and say:  You can’t attack us; we’re going to build a nuclear weapon and there’s nothing you can do about it, because we have so many missiles and so many drones that if you try to do anything about our nuclear program, we will wipe out every country in the Middle East; we will drive the U.S. forces out of the region; we can do whatever we want. 

That is what they were trying to achieve.  The President of the United States, Donald J. Trump, was never going to allow that to happen.  He just wasn’t.  He addressed something that had been ignored for far too long.  And so, he destroyed their drone program, their drone manufacturing capability.  He destroyed their missile capability.  He severely eroded both of those capabilities in terms of current launchers.  He destroyed their navy; he destroyed their air force.  They are far less powerful militarily today than they were, and that line of immunity they were trying to hide behind has been erased.  They will never have a nuclear weapon, period, not as long as President Trump is in office.  And that, to us, is the bright line. 

Now, how you achieve that and go forth, I think we’ve got multiple opportunities in the past to reach agreement on those things, and they have failed to do so.  Now they’re facing crippling sanctions.  Their economy is in total and complete freefall.  I’m happy that for the first time, even the media in the U.S. is beginning to cover what a bad situation Iran faces.  The Straits of Hormuz are open.  There’s always as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began, so they’ve lost complete control of the straits.  And their economy – and it’s not – not only are they in freefall now – the Iranian economy is about to reach a place that few countries in the world have been in terms of how bad it’s going to get. 

And it’s all the fault – all the fault – of the radical Shia clerics that make the decisions in that country.  They are the ones that will put the poor people of Iran in the situation that they’re in, because every dollar and every penny that that regime gets, they don’t spend it on roads or bridges or helping improve the lives of the Iranian people.  They spend that money on Hizballah and Hamas and militias that fire rockets out of Iraq – and the Houthis.  That’s who they spend their money on.  They should have spent their money on their people, and instead they spend their money on terrorism and on weapons.  So, hopefully that’ll change.  But – yeah, they’ll never have a nuclear weapon.

QUESTION:  To the foreign minister, if I may.  To the foreign minister —

MODERATOR:  Excuse me.  No, I believe you had your fair share.  We need to proceed with the next questioner. 

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  That’s okay, if they want. 

MODERATOR:  Unless my minister —

QUESTION:  Thank you.  Thank you very much, Mr. Foreign Minister, for taking the question.  As President Trump weighs the potential of renewed strikes on Iran, is consideration being given in Greece to support those strikes from Souda Bay, especially in light of the events at Fairford that demonstrated increased Iranian threats to U.S. assets in Europe?  Thank you.

As I was already mentioned, Greece is already a major player in the Red Sea operation under the (inaudible) of the European Union, the speediest operation for the safe navigation of vessels passed through the Red Sea.  If it is necessary to participate in additional operations and a framework of greater cooperation that will be (inaudible) passage from the Gulf, it is obvious that Greece will once again be at the forefront. 

MODERATOR:  (Via interpreter) Next question. 

QUESTION:  (Via interpreter) Good morning.  Vassilis Nedos, Kathimerini newspaper.  My question is to the minister of foreign affairs.  You’ve already mentioned the operations in which Greece participates in the Red Sea.  There are many open and clear requests from the U.S. side for participation in other U.S. initiatives in the Middle East – Hormuz, Red Sea – in the greater regions (inaudible) as well as Greece in terms of participating in such missions.  And I wanted to ask you whether you discussed the (inaudible) Greece’s relationship and how this is affecting (inaudible).  

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  (In Greek.)

MODERATOR:  And one last question, please.  I would like to stress the “one” because we are a bit behind schedule.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Good luck.  (Laughter.) 

MODERATOR:  Please. 

QUESTION:  Thank you, John Hudson with the Washington Post.  Mr. Secretary, will the State Department continue telling foreign governments not to facilitate Maria Carina Machado’s return to Venezuela?  And a bigger societal question —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What?  What are – I can’t – what are you saying?  You’re talking like an auctioneer.  Slow down.

QUESTION:  (Laughter.)  I’m just trying to make sure I get everything in.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  He’s trying – he’s talking fast because he’s trying to get another question in. 

QUESTION:  You —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What was your first question?

QUESTION:  That is correct.  (Laughter.)  Will the State Department continue telling foreign governments not to —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Who told you we said that?

QUESTION:  That’s widely reported at this point.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It is?  By who?  Who widely reported that?

QUESTION:  Wall Street Journal has —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh.  So, if it’s in the newspaper, it’s true?  Because I can show you a lot of articles that are in the newspaper that are not true.  So, this is – I always love these stories.  You guys get somebody to tell you something, then you report it so now it’s an established fact, and then you ask me about it as if somehow I’m responding to something that’s been factually proven.  I don’t know what you’re talking about.  Honestly, I don’t know.  Just because you guys report something doesn’t mean it’s true.  You know this, right?  I’m sure you know this.  Okay. So, the premise of your question is not true.

We’ve never asked anyone not to let anybody else in anywhere in the world.  I’ve told – I’ve said this repeatedly about – so I don’t – I know how to answer a question that’s based on something that is false.

QUESTION:  Well, how about a bigger societal question —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, okay. 

QUESTION:  — on artificial intelligence?  Where do you stand on the government’s role?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It’s called super intelligence.

QUESTION:  I figured you might challenge that —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay, all right. 

QUESTION:  — that language.  Where do you stand on the government’s role in preventing Frontier Labs from threatening the future of the human race?  And Mr. Minister, where does Greece and the European Union stand on regulating American AI companies?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, we have – just on super – it doesn’t matter where I stand on it.  It’s not about where I stand – where does the U.S. Government – the U.S. Government has set up a process, as you know.  Jay Clayton is running that task force, and it’s going to establish how the U.S. is going to interact with attempts to regulate, attempts to mitigate against the potential downsides of super intelligence, but also the ability to benefit from the good things that it’s going to do. 

So, we’ve got a task force set up that he’s chairing, and it has a good group of people involved in it.  And there’s where you’re going to find the – and look, this is a new issue.  I mean, it’s not a new issue, but it’s an issue that’s rapidly evolved in terms of the consciousness of people and nation-states having to address it.  And we’ve stood up a process to do that, as far as the U.S. response is concerned.  And we’ll work very closely with our allies around the world as well.

So, I would just refer you to that process and that task force as it begins its work.  You saw what the President did last week when they had a gathering of all the leaders in that field.  They had a joint declaration that sort of laid out some very broad outlines as to how we’re going to approach this.  And the goal is this, as best I could describe it in the most simplistic terms.  Super intelligence is going to happen – or what people call AI – is going to happen, okay?  It’s happening already.  Here’s the question:  How do we take the positives of it and harness it in a way that serves the interests of our country?  And how do we mitigate or prevent the dangers of it? 

And to begin, you have to understand what are the potential benefits and what are the potential downsides.  And then what role can government play in terms of a regulatory structure to influence those two things?  Highlighting and making sure the positives are enjoyed by our country, mitigating against the dangers, that’s what this process is designed to do, and they’re working very quickly, and they have to work very quickly because that technology is evolving extremely fast.

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  (In Greek.)

MODERATOR:  Thank you very much.  This concludes the joint press statements and the press avail.

QUESTION:  Thank you. 

MODERATOR:  I will kindly ask that you remain seated for a few minutes.

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  (In Greek.)  Thank you so much.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.

Trump, was never going to allow that to happen.  He just wasn’t.  He addressed something that had been ignored for far too long.  And so, he destroyed their drone program, their drone manufacturing capability.  He destroyed their missile capability.  He severely eroded both of those capabilities in terms of current launchers.  He destroyed their navy; he destroyed their air force.  They are far less powerful militarily today than they were, and that line of immunity they were trying to hide behind has been erased.  They will never have a nuclear weapon, period, not as long as President Trump is in office.  And that, to us, is the bright line.

As I was already mentioned, Greece is already a major player in the Red Sea operation under the (inaudible) of the European Union, the speediest operation for the safe navigation of vessels passed through the Red Sea.  If it is necessary to participate in additional operations and a framework of greater cooperation that will be (inaudible) passage from the Gulf, it is obvious that Greece will once again be at the forefront.

QUESTION:  (Via interpreter) Good morning.  Vassilis Nedos, Kathimerini newspaper.  My question is to the minister of foreign affairs.  You’ve already mentioned the operations in which Greece participates in the Red Sea.  There are many open and clear requests from the U.S. side for participation in other U.S. initiatives in the Middle East – Hormuz, Red Sea – in the greater regions (inaudible) as well as Greece in terms of participating in such missions.  And I wanted to ask you whether you discussed the (inaudible) Greece’s relationship and how this is affecting (inaudible).  

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  (In Greek.)

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Good luck.  (Laughter.)

QUESTION:  (Laughter.)  I’m just trying to make sure I get everything in.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  He’s trying – he’s talking fast because he’s trying to get another question in. 

QUESTION:  You —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What was your first question?

QUESTION:  That is correct.  (Laughter.)  Will the State Department continue telling foreign governments not to —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Who told you we said that?

QUESTION:  That’s widely reported at this point.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It is?  By who?  Who widely reported that?

And to begin, you have to understand what are the potential benefits and what are the potential downsides.  And then what role can government play in terms of a regulatory structure to influence those two things?  Highlighting and making sure the positives are enjoyed by our country, mitigating against the dangers, that’s what this process is designed to do, and they’re working very quickly, and they have to work very quickly because that technology is evolving extremely fast.

MODERATOR:  I will kindly ask that you remain seated for a few minutes.

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  (In Greek.)  Thank you so much.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the U.S. Embassy Chancery Dedication Ceremony
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Athens, Greece

U.S. Embassy

Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the U.S. Embassy Chancery Dedication Ceremony

Remarks

October 7, 2026

AMBASSADOR GUILFOYLE:  Kalimera.  Secretary Rubio, Your Grace Bishop (inaudible), colleagues from Washington and from this mission, good afternoon.  Today is truly a special day for the United States Embassy in Greece as we inaugurate our new chancellor.  In a country where the history of democracy lies beneath our feet, we are proud to dedicate this new building where we work hard every day on behalf of the American people.  This ceremony dedicates a building, but it also renews our purpose to advance American interests, protect American lives, and strengthen our alliance.

There is no greater honor than to open this new chapter in American diplomacy with our 72nd Secretary of State and National Security Advisor – and my dear friend – Marco Rubio.  Secretary Rubio is a true friend of Greece, and he is a champion of democracy.  Throughout his distinguished career, he has stood shoulder to shoulder with our allies to defend liberty across the globe.  His visit today shows that the United States-Greece partnership is more vibrant and more vital than ever.  Secretary Rubio has been the strongest and the most steadfast supporter of this important relationship for many, many years, going back to his days in the Senate.  It is only fitting that he is here to commemorate this historic moment in the history of the United States Diplomatic Mission to Greece.

I am also deeply touched that His Grace the Bishop Theofilestatos Varnavas has joined us today.  The Greek Orthodox Church plays an extraordinary role in the spiritual life of both the United States and Greece.  Your presence reminds us that everything we do at this mission serves a higher purpose.  I now invite His Grace to offer a blessing, followed by remarks from Secretary Rubio.  Thank you, God bless you, God bless Greece, and may God bless the United States of America.

(The blessing was made.)

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I didn’t want to hurt anyone.  (Laughter.)  I’m going after (inaudible).  How am I supposed to follow that?  (Laughter.)  Thank you, (inaudible).  Thank you so much.  Thank you, Your Grace, for this.  Thank you, Ambassador, for hosting.  Thank you all for being here.  It’s – this is one of the Department of State’s most impressive and historic embassies.  (Inaudible) to engage in diplomacy with one of our key allies in the world, and I want to thank all of you for doing this, and thank you again for blessing this new workplace.  I also want to recognize the five American public servants who have died in the line of duty, victims of the brutal reign of violence of (inaudible) terrorist groups. 

Our embassies are more than just buildings.  They’re architectural reflections of our country.  I mean, that is the first impression that we make in many cases on our host nation.  But they also have (inaudible) functional.  They should keep the staff inside safe, and they should secure the sensitive documents and the conversations that protect American citizens wherever they are in the world. 

But stylistically, when appropriate, they should be designed in a uniquely American way.  They should show strength.  They should show leadership and an openness to engagement.  And this embassy with this marble – it’s the same marble that was used to build the Parthenon – reflects our cultural ties to the region and our reverence for the city’s history and influence on our own nation’s institutions.  The completion of these renovations renews that acknowledgement for the ties we share with this land, and also to the high esteem in which we hold the city’s great monuments.

But of course, an embassy is just an empty building without the contents.  The completion of these renovations at last bring back together all the embassy staff who have been held at other locations during the years of the construction.  Many of you have been offsite for (inaudible) years now, and we in the Department are grateful for your flexibility and your patience during this prolonged process. 

I’m very proud to be the Secretary to participate in the ribbon-cutting ceremony, and I hope that this building will continue to foster the strong relations between the United States and our host nation, Greece.  And just as the Parthenon inspired your architect’s design of this building over 60 years ago, may the history, artifacts, and (inaudible) ruins of the city’s ancient civilization inspire us to remember – and never to forget – our proud Western heritage and values as we conduct our work here.  So, thank you.  (Applause.)

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis at the Opening Session of the United States-Greece Strategic Dialogue
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greek Foreign Minister
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Giorgos Gerapetritis, Greek Foreign Minister

Athens, Greece

Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis at the Opening Session of the United States-Greece Strategic Dialogue

Remarks

October 7, 2026

FOREIGN MINISTER GERAPETRITIS:  Dear Secretary, dear colleagues, it is a great pleasure to welcome and your delegation to Athens for the sixth round of the Greece-U.S. Strategic Dialogue.  Your presence here speaks to the enduring strength of our relationship and to the importance both our countries attach to its future.   

Since the launch of the Strategic Dialogue back in 2018, our cooperation has grown steadily in scope and ambition, encompassing defense, energy, infrastructure, digital technologies, law enforcement, maritime affairs, and the close ties between our peoples.  The three agreements signed today are tangible evidence of that progress.  Our partnership has never been stronger, deeper, or more consequential.  It rests on shared values and a common determination to advance peace, stability, security, and prosperity for our peoples, for our regions, and beyond.   

We meet at a time of profound geopolitical change.  The ongoing war in Ukraine, instability in the Middle East, threats to maritime security in the Red Sea, and the resurgence of a revisionist rhetoric demand resolve, coordination, and a clear sense of purpose.  In this uncertain environment, Greece remains a reliable ally and an anchor of stability in the Eastern Mediterranean.  During the 2025-‘26 term on the United Nations – of the Security Council – and as we prepare to assume the presidency of the Council of the European Union second semester of 2027 – we bring that same sense of responsibility to our work.  Respect for international law is a guiding principle for our foreign policy and an essential condition for lasting peace.   

Greece’s geography places us at the meeting point of three continents.  Our history, our longstanding relationships across the region, and the enduring influence of Hellenism allow us to engage with a wide range of partners in good faith and with credibility.  This gives Greece a particular responsibility and a practical capacity to connect countries, facilitate dialogue, and build understanding.  It also gives our partnership strategic value.  Strengthening Greece’s role strengthens the security of the wider region and advances interests we share with the United States.   

The Strategic Dialogue allow us to translate this convergence into concrete action.  Today, we have an opportunity to carry that world forward across its core pillars.  Our defense cooperation has reached unprecedented levels.  The Mutual Defense Cooperation Agreement has deepened our strategic partnership and strengthened our capacity to address common security challenges.   

Alexandroupolis exemplifies the value of this cooperation.  A sovereign Greek port and a vital logistical hub for the United States, it contributes directly to the security of nations – of NATO’s eastern flank.  Greece’s consistently high defense expenditure and longstanding contribution to the Alliance reflect a simple conviction:  Collective security requires every Ally to shoulder its responsibilities.  We are committed to further strengthening our defense cooperation, including through procurement, industrial partnerships, and advanced technologies.  Our growing collaboration in law enforcement and counterterrorism is equally important to the security of our citizens.   

On energy, Greece is emerging as a vital hub for Southeastern and Central Europe infrastructure, such as the Alexandroupolis FSRU.  Together with our leading role in the Vertical Corridor, this diversifying supply is strengthening resilience and giving our neighbors greater energy security.  The growing engagement of U.S. energy companies, including Severn and ExxonMobil, underscores confidence, increases potential, (inaudible) the opportunities our partnership offers.   

Our maritime strength are the third strategic dimension.  With Greek-owned vessels accounting for almost one-fourth of global energy shipping capacity globally, Greek shipping plays a pivotal role in connecting energy producers with consumers and sustaining transatlantic energy flows.  The transformation of the Greek economy has opened a new chapter in our bilateral relationship.  Renewed growth and investment confidence are creating opportunities for American businesses to participate in Greece’s progress.   

Investment by leading U.S. technology companies in data centers’ digital infrastructure is helping to establish Greece as a regional center for innovation.  Our ambition is to build on this momentum through partnerships that create skilled jobs, support research, and bring new opportunities to the next generation.   

At the heart of this relationship, however, are our people.  The Greek American community has helped shape America while sustaining a close and abiding connection with Greece.  Its achievements in business, science, public service, and the arts are a source of pride for both our nations.  Greek Americans have made Greece’s heritage part of America’s success.  They embody a relationship rooted in the ideals of liberty, democracy, and the rule of law, ideals that inspired America’s Founding Fathers and continue to give our partnership purpose.  Our expanding education and cultural exchanges carry this connection forward, allowing young Greeks and Americans to learn from one another and to build relationships of their own.   

Mr. Secretary, I look forward to our discussions today and to the practical results that we deliver.  We have a strong foundation and a clear sense of what we can achieve.  Today’s discussion will help us turn that shared ambition into practical results.  Our alliance draws strength – draws strength from all we have achieved together.  Its promise lies in what we choose to do next.  Thank you. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, thank you.  Thank you for this opportunity to be here today for the sixth time a U.S. secretary of state gathers with their counterparts in Greece for this Strategic Dialogue.  And I’m happy to be here in Greece for that dialogue.  It’s my first trip to the country ever; I didn’t even have a chance to come as a senator.  And so I’m happy to be here and to be a part of this Strategic Dialogue.   

I want to begin by saying that I hope our presence here today and our work that we’re about to do – and continue to do together – highlights something very important, and that is how critical the historic alliance between Greece and the United States is.  And this is especially true now at a time of great global uncertainty, whether it’s the war between Russia and Ukraine, whether it’s what’s happening in the Middle East, whether it’s – meaning in the Straits of Hormuz and, increasingly now, in the Red Sea because of the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.   

At a time of extraordinary global tumult and global instability, we need anchor partners rooted in a common history.  And that is what Greece has meant for the United States and, I hope, what the United States has meant for Greece and what we will continue to mean for each other.  This strong partnership, it’s a relationship that spans a variety of fronts – obviously defense and security, our mutual defense and security as allies and partners, but it extends to trade, to investment, to energy.  There literally is no – it’s a cultural exchange.  There are literally no areas of our societies or of our countries that are not part of the U.S.-Greece relationship, and we seek to build and expand on every single one of them.   

Let me begin by saying what is obvious to everyone but should continue to be obvious:  Greece is an indispensable NATO partner, an indispensable NATO Ally.  It is a pillar of stability in this region, it is a pillar of the U.S.’s presence in this region, and it is a pillar of how we secure our national interest as well as Greece’s in the region.  So we are thrilled – part of that, some of the things that aren’t heavily perceived but we’ll be able to be a part of announcing again later today, is we’re thrilled that Greece joins the

U.S. National Guard Bureau of State Sponsorship Program, and they’re doing so with the guard from my home state of Florida.  It’s another milestone in our deepening defense relationship. 

The U.S.-Greece Economic Security Declaration commits both nations to continue to work with likeminded allies as well to develop secure supply chains.  That includes – including critical mineral productions, again another area of very strong cooperation in which our mutual interests are aligned but also in which we’re taking concrete action. 

Our energy relationship is reaching new heights, and it continues to expand and grow, and it’s something we’re going to be building on.  The Vertical Gas Corridor expansion has cemented in Greece, has cemented Greece as an energy hub and as a secure energy hub, and has facilitated increase in U.S. LNG exports to Europe.  That’s something we continue to build on. 

Our bilateral relationship as countries, of course, at the end, is founded not just in a common history but in enduring ties of family, of culture, of religion, of a shared heritage.  As I’ll speak about later today in what I think is a pretty historic setting, from what I read – (laughter) – it – we are indebted to ancient Greece for its role in shaping not just our country but, frankly, our civilization. 

And we – so we’re here today to remember the past because that’s the foundation upon which our relationship is built, but also to focus on the future, because we have incredible things that we can do together.  And I’m very grateful to be a part of this, to be – excited to be a part of the Strategic Dialogue and happy to be here on my first visit to Greece but hopefully not my last.

Partnership

The Strategic Dialogue allow us to translate this convergence into concrete action.  Today, we have an opportunity to carry that world forward across its core pillars.  Our defense cooperation has reached unprecedented levels.  The Mutual Defense Cooperation Agreement has deepened our strategic partnership and strengthened our capacity to address common security challenges.   

Alexandroupolis exemplifies the value of this cooperation.  A sovereign Greek port and a vital logistical hub for the United States, it contributes directly to the security of nations – of NATO’s eastern flank.  Greece’s consistently high defense expenditure and longstanding contribution to the Alliance reflect a simple conviction:  Collective security requires every Ally to shoulder its responsibilities.  We are committed to further strengthening our defense cooperation, including through procurement, industrial partnerships, and advanced technologies.  Our growing collaboration in law enforcement and counterterrorism is equally important to the security of our citizens.   

On energy, Greece is emerging as a vital hub for Southeastern and Central Europe infrastructure, such as the Alexandroupolis FSRU.  Together with our leading role in the Vertical Corridor, this diversifying supply is strengthening resilience and giving our neighbors greater energy security.  The growing engagement of U.S. energy companies, including Severn and ExxonMobil, underscores confidence, increases potential, (inaudible) the opportunities our partnership offers.   

Our maritime strength are the third strategic dimension.  With Greek-owned vessels accounting for almost one-fourth of global energy shipping capacity globally, Greek shipping plays a pivotal role in connecting energy producers with consumers and sustaining transatlantic energy flows.  The transformation of the Greek economy has opened a new chapter in our bilateral relationship.  Renewed growth and investment confidence are creating opportunities for American businesses to participate in Greece’s progress.   

Investment by leading U.S. technology companies in data centers’ digital infrastructure is helping to establish Greece as a regional center for innovation.  Our ambition is to build on this momentum through partnerships that create skilled jobs, support research, and bring new opportunities to the next generation.   

At the heart of this relationship, however, are our people.  The Greek American community has helped shape America while sustaining a close and abiding connection with Greece.  Its achievements in business, science, public service, and the arts are a source of pride for both our nations.  Greek Americans have made Greece’s heritage part of America’s success.  They embody a relationship rooted in the ideals of liberty, democracy, and the rule of law, ideals that inspired America’s Founding Fathers and continue to give our partnership purpose.  Our expanding education and cultural exchanges carry this connection forward, allowing young Greeks and Americans to learn from one another and to build relationships of their own.   

Mr. Secretary, I look forward to our discussions today and to the practical results that we deliver.  We have a strong foundation and a clear sense of what we can achieve.  Today’s discussion will help us turn that shared ambition into practical results.  Our alliance draws strength – draws strength from all we have achieved together.  Its promise lies in what we choose to do next.  Thank you. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, thank you.  Thank you for this opportunity to be here today for the sixth time a U.S. secretary of state gathers with their counterparts in Greece for this Strategic Dialogue.  And I’m happy to be here in Greece for that dialogue.  It’s my first trip to the country ever; I didn’t even have a chance to come as a senator.  And so I’m happy to be here and to be a part of this Strategic Dialogue.   

I want to begin by saying that I hope our presence here today and our work that we’re about to do – and continue to do together – highlights something very important, and that is how critical the historic alliance between Greece and the United States is.  And this is especially true now at a time of great global uncertainty, whether it’s the war between Russia and Ukraine, whether it’s what’s happening in the Middle East, whether it’s – meaning in the Straits of Hormuz and, increasingly now, in the Red Sea because of the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.   

At a time of extraordinary global tumult and global instability, we need anchor partners rooted in a common history.  And that is what Greece has meant for the United States and, I hope, what the United States has meant for Greece and what we will continue to mean for each other.  This strong partnership, it’s a relationship that spans a variety of fronts – obviously defense and security, our mutual defense and security as allies and partners, but it extends to trade, to investment, to energy.  There literally is no – it’s a cultural exchange.  There are literally no areas of our societies or of our countries that are not part of the U.S.-Greece relationship, and we seek to build and expand on every single one of them.   

Let me begin by saying what is obvious to everyone but should continue to be obvious:  Greece is an indispensable NATO partner, an indispensable NATO Ally.  It is a pillar of stability in this region, it is a pillar of the U.S.’s presence in this region, and it is a pillar of how we secure our national interest as well as Greece’s in the region.  So we are thrilled – part of that, some of the things that aren’t heavily perceived but we’ll be able to be a part of announcing again later today, is we’re thrilled that Greece joins the

U.S. National Guard Bureau of State Sponsorship Program, and they’re doing so with the guard from my home state of Florida.  It’s another milestone in our deepening defense relationship. 

The U.S.-Greece Economic Security Declaration commits both nations to continue to work with likeminded allies as well to develop secure supply chains.  That includes – including critical mineral productions, again another area of very strong cooperation in which our mutual interests are aligned but also in which we’re taking concrete action. 

Our energy relationship is reaching new heights, and it continues to expand and grow, and it’s something we’re going to be building on.  The Vertical Gas Corridor expansion has cemented in Greece, has cemented Greece as an energy hub and as a secure energy hub, and has facilitated increase in U.S. LNG exports to Europe.  That’s something we continue to build on. 

Our bilateral relationship as countries, of course, at the end, is founded not just in a common history but in enduring ties of family, of culture, of religion, of a shared heritage.  As I’ll speak about later today in what I think is a pretty historic setting, from what I read – (laughter) – it – we are indebted to ancient Greece for its role in shaping not just our country but, frankly, our civilization. 

And we – so we’re here today to remember the past because that’s the foundation upon which our relationship is built, but also to focus on the future, because we have incredible things that we can do together.  And I’m very grateful to be a part of this, to be – excited to be a part of the Strategic Dialogue and happy to be here on my first visit to Greece but hopefully not my last.

Partnership

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir at a Joint Press Availability
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, Icelandic Foreign Minister
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, Icelandic Foreign Minister

Reykjavik, Iceland

Safnahúsið

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir at a Joint Press Availability

Remarks

October 6, 2026

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  (In Icelandic.)  Thank you all for being here.  I will not continue in Icelandic, my dear Marco, and thank you especially for visiting Iceland.  I think that demonstrates also very well our close connections and good relationship.  And it has actually been, from my point of view, a productive morning.  I would say so.  We started, as you know, at Hofdi House, where we first had the opportunity to hear about the historic summit back almost 40 years ago between President Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev, and I hope you enjoyed our meeting in Hofdi.  I thought there’s a kind of special atmosphere there.

The Secretary and I, then we had an excellent bilateral meeting at Hofdi, and now, just now, we concluded a very good meeting with – here in Safnahusid with our prime minister here in Iceland, Kristrún Frostadóttir.  I would say throughout our discussions, they have been good and it has been very clear that Iceland and U.S., the United States of America, we enjoy a very good and strong and also enduring friendship.  We share a long history.  The U.S. was – as we have already mentioned, the U.S. was the first country to recognize the Republic of Iceland back in 1944.  We are both founding members of NATO 1949, and of course we have the valuable bilateral Defense Agreement between our two countries since 1951. 

And we are working closely together every day here in Iceland, especially to safeguard the security of the High North, North Atlantic, and the Arctic.  For us, being a credible and responsible ally, we take this role very seriously here in Iceland, especially when it comes to the U.S. and the whole of NATO.  And this is also very much and strongly reflected in our new policy – and actually the first one – policy and defense and security.  It also strongly emphasizes the very important relationship through defense and security with the U.S.  

With Iceland and the U.S. both being Arctic nations, the Secretary and I, we fully agreed on the need to work together to ensure a safe and secure Arctic region.  And I especially want to commend you, Marco, on how you have taken such a strong initiative to – in making the A7, Arctic 7 group, even more effective than it has been before.  And that matters for us here in Iceland a lot.

And we also discussed the agreement that has been found between the U.S., Greenland, and Denmark, and that is also hugely important for the region that we got this good agreement on Greenland.

As we discussed also in both our meetings now today, there are ample opportunities to deepen our economic and investment relations even further – for instance, in geothermal energy.  We discussed data centers, pharmaceuticals, as well as digital and other infrastructure.  And we also talked about the challenging global context, which is on our minds as Russia full-scale invasion in Ukraine – very brutal, very relentless.  And we touched on the dire situation in the Middle East and also we discussed our relations to China. 

But above all, the Secretary and I, we had productive and constructive discussions, conversation, and I think the message is very clear.  We are allies, we are friends, and we will continue working very closely to strengthen and deepen our good relationship. 

So over to you, dear Marco.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, thank you for welcoming here – us here.  This is a place that many Americans visit.  I think the number that was shared with us as coming in and here today is over 700,000 Americans.  Our great ambassador, who’s only been here a couple months but is already doing a great job – so he’s going to get that up to a million American visitors over the next few years, but – with direct flights from multiple cities.  And now we see why people want to come here.  It’s a beautiful country, a wonderful people, the most peaceful country in the world.  It’s one of the safest countries in the world, a country that’s also blessed with abundance of energy that is renewable and self-sustaining. 

And so you have so many good things coming and going in your direction, and we’re so happy to be a close partner of yours, as we have been for a very long time.  We have tremendous respect for your – the people, and we have tremendous respect for the country and the role that it plays, and it has for a very long time.  I mean, for decades this nation in Iceland has occupied a critical strategic position for our collective security, and that remains true today more than ever before. 

And while the world’s focus drifted over the last 20 years, the reality is the geography is always important, and we’re seeing that come now to fruition.  The location of this country between the United States and Europe and the High North means that it sits at the – Iceland sits at the center of many of the questions surrounding the security and the defense of our shared region. 

And today those threats are growing, which is why this focus on the Arctic in general and Iceland in particular is so critical.  Our potential adversaries and real competitors already – and the predatory industries associated with them – are already acting as – against our interests.  And so it’s important that we continue to cooperate in the security realm the way we are doing and continue to do. 

Obviously I think one of the unique aspects of the country – in a positive way, I think – is that you don’t have a traditional military in the traditional sense of the word, but as – but you are a NATO member and you are a contributor to collective security, and you continue to contribute that critical role in our Alliance and share the burden of defending region.  And in practice, what that means and has meant for a very long time is you welcoming NATO Allies to come here and to operate jointly within Icelandic territory, and we want to continue to build upon that as a way to prevent conflict – not as a way to encourage conflict or provoke conflict, but prevent it. 

History teaches us that deterrence is the best prevention of violence and the best preventer of war.  And you play such – have played such a strategic role in the past and continue to play that now.  So since the Second World War, Iceland has allowed the U.S. military to project power and collectively working together, using your land, your air, your sea; giving us a critical outpost for monitoring clandestine behavior and deterring our adversaries from entering your sovereign territory and the sovereign territory of our mutual allies. 

This year marks the 75th anniversary of the 1951 U.S.-Iceland Defense Agreement.  And I’m proud to say that our military and our Icelandic partners continue to work together to secure this land and the waters that surround it.  Just last month, over 1,200 Americans participated along with our allies in the Northern Viking 2026 military exercise, something that’s occurred every year and will continue to occur.

And – but I want to talk a little bit beyond the military and security domain, because Iceland is not just an important security partner; it is a critical partner in our mutual economic interests for the foreseeable future.  Your landscapes, for example, have been the training ground for American astronauts since the Appollo program and continues to host training missions for the Artemis missions.  Your expertise in geothermal energy and biotechnology and marine industries, those present incredible opportunities for greater commercial and technological cooperation. 

We discussed that today and our efforts to perhaps – we are going to work now on building out a group of American industries and present them to investment opportunities that exist here, and likewise identify for your companies here investment opportunities that may exist in the United States.  That’s how you continue to build upon the economic bonds that lead to our shared prosperity and our mutual prosperity, so that’s important.  So today we discussed concrete ideas about how we can deepen cooperation in these fields and further strengthen our robust bilateral relationship to benefit our people. 

So I really look forward to – as I said, we had an opportunity to engage in Ankara earlier this year.  I told you I would be coming soon, and I’m here now and I’m happy to have come.  This is my first visit here in any capacity.  I believe – and we discussed this earlier – it’s probably the first bilateral visit by a secretary of state in a very long time.  I know Secretary Blinken had been here as part of a broader gathering earlier, but – and maybe we’ll be able to – but this, I think this is the first time a secretary of state comes in a long time in terms of a bilateral visit, and perhaps it won’t be the last one because of how much esteem we have for your country, for your government, for your people, and for the importance of this relationship.

So really, really happy to be here, really glad I came.  And now I know, just in the limited things I’ve gotten to see – because obviously there’s only so much you can see through the window of a hotel and the window of a car, but you can see why people fall in love with this country and you can see why Americans are fascinated by it, and we want to build upon that both in the tourism sector, in the economic sector, and in our enduring security cooperation.

So thank you for hosting me, for hosting us, and thank you for this opportunity to interact with you. 

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you, dear Marco.  And actually you saw – witnessed the Northern Lights yesterday.  You told me. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I did.  Which, as someone from Florida —

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Yeah.  (Laughter.) 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  — I didn’t know if that was a UFO or what it was, but then I looked at it and I realized what it was pretty quickly.  It was very special. 

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you, Marco.  Who is going to conduct – yes, yeah. 

MODERATOR:  Thank you.  And we’ll take a few questions from the media now, starting with the Icelandic press.  Mr. Hallgrímur Indridason from RUV, the Icelandic broadcasting service.

QUESTION:  Thank you.  The first question from RUV:  In light of the deal that the U.S., Greenland, and Denmark made on Greenland defenses, which included buildup, like, in two more military bases in Greenland, are there any plans for the U.S. Government to have further buildup here in Iceland, whether these are its military base or more surveillance or anything of that sort?  Are you increasing your presence in Iceland and —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  And the second question from – on behalf of Radio Saga:  Do you feel that Iceland poses a direct military threat from Russia?  And if so, what makes Iceland vulnerable in that area? 

And if I may add a short yes-or-no question, what is your position on NATO membership of Ukraine?  Do you think Ukraine should be a member of NATO?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, just on your third point, there’s no yes-or-no answer to that other than to say that Ukraine – right now, NATO membership, as you know, is not on the table as we speak, because there’s obviously a consensus process that has to happen in order for that, a unanimity process that has to happen.  Right now, we’re simply focused, when it comes to Ukraine, on the ending of this conflict if that’s possible.  And it’s unfortunate the amount of loss of life.  We’ve been clear that if there’s a role we can play in bringing that war to an end, we want to play a constructive role.  We are obviously watching the trend lines there and seeing that’s not the direction that it’s headed right now.

On your first question which has to do – well, I forgot your first question because you guys, you’re cheating.  (Laughter.)  You said it was one question and then you got three, so now I gotta write these down. 

QUESTION:  Military buildup.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, military build – well look, we’d never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what’s available.  I think there is a willingness to do more together.  And what Iceland contributes really is infrastructure and technology and the ability to have surveillance and opportunity of domain awareness.  And it wouldn’t be anything new.  I mean, it’s already existed for a very long time.  We obviously had an enduring presence here that ended in 2006, not because of anything that was going wrong but because we shifted forces to other parts of the world where we thought there was more crisis. 

The reality of it is the world has changed over the last 20 years.  Our focus has changed.  There’s a lot of focus on the Arctic.  I think Iceland plays a very critical role in the defense of NATO writ large.  I think Iceland and its location plays a critical role in the defense both of Europe but also of the homeland of the United States because of geography.  So we would be open to having those conversations to see what more we can do together.  I know there’s interest in doing more together.  And obviously, if there’s opportunities that make sense for both countries, it’s something we would pursue.

With regards to direct threats, look, at the end of the day I think we’re all concerned about what’s happening in the High North and in the Arctic region, both from irregular measures, covert measures that are happening, but also threats to undersea cables, threats to shipping lanes.  We’re all aware of it, which is why so much attention is being paid to the Arctic region.  And it’s something that we have to deal with collectively, not just alone unilaterally but in combination with our partners and allies, which is why we’ve been having these regular engagements with the Arctic 7 countries, and Iceland is a key component of that and a place where we’ve already had a history of cooperating on these matters in the past.

So yeah, I mean, there are direct threats, and those threats in the 21st century aren’t just military threats.  They’re also economic and commercial threats that have implications on the national security of our respective countries.

MODERATOR:  Thank you, Mr. Secretary.  Next we will go to Richard Crowley from The New York Times.

QUESTION:  Thank you.  Michael Crowley with —

MODERATOR:  Michael, I’m sorry. 

QUESTION:  No problem – with The New York Times.  Thank you, Mr. Secretary.  My questions were going to be similar, so just keying off of what you were just asked.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  All right, good, so you don’t need your time for the same —

QUESTION:  No such luck. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  All right, go ahead.  What’s your backup question?

QUESTION:  Regarding Northern Viking, although there was U.S. participation for the first time in the history of those exercises, the U.S. did not participate with ships or airplanes, which I saw was noticed in regional coverage about those exercises.  Is that significant?  Do you want to explain why that might have been the case?

And last month, there was a diplomatic incident when the Iceland foreign ministry summoned the ambassador over a post by the President on social media which depicted a map showing several nations in the region colored in with American stars and stripes, including Canada, Greenland, and also Iceland.  I wondered if you wanted to comment on the significance of that and anything you may have said in your trip here today.

And for the prime minister —

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Foreign.

QUESTION:  — did you find the absence of American forces —

MODERATOR:  Foreign minister.

QUESTION:  Pardon me.  Foreign Minister, do you find the absence of American forces in the Northern Viking exercises to be meaningful or worrisome at all?  And do you have any comment that you want to make about the social media posting, and are you concerned that you could be facing a drama like the one that Greenland recently went through with President Trump as far as talk of American acquisition?  Thank you, and my apology for misstating your title.  Thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  That’s an unforgivable error.  I mean, I don’t even know if I should answer your question after doing that.  (Laughter.)

Look, on the second point, we’re not talking about social media posts.  I’m here – we’re here – meeting with a country we work very closely together on, and we do a lot of things together and everything is very positive in our relationship. 

So on the first point about ships and airplanes, look, obviously there’s things going on around the world.  That’s not a mystery to anyone.  It requires us to allocate resources.  And sometimes when you are involved, whether it’s in protecting shipping lanes like we’ve had to do in the – because of this terrorist regime in Iran targeting commercial shipping lanes, or the defense of airspace, or the need to backfill what’s happening in the Indo-Pacific as a result of this shift of forces – anytime you have active activities going on in the world, you have to move your assets to that, and sometimes they’re not available for exercises. 

So it’s – I don’t think that’s an enduring decision.  I think just one that, from the timing standpoint of when it happened, and it overlayed with existing operations around the world.  So – but I don’t think that’s enduring.  We still had people present.  We’re still committed to it.  And as I said, I’m visiting here today because this place matters both economically but also from a defense standpoint.

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Yeah, actually, I have nothing to add to this.  He explained – Marco explained very eloquently during our meeting why they needed the forces elsewhere.  And I want to underline our really strong cooperation in terms of defense and security, and there is no change in that – what that matters.

What matters about the tweet or the posting from Mr. President, from President Trump, we discussed that, and I mean we have already dealt with that constructively.  And we are actually – and yes, you are right, I summoned the ambassador.  We were very open about this because we have a very good relationship with the U.S., and we want to continue to build on that relationship. 

So that’s why we remain now focused on the future, on the strong and positive relationship between our two countries.  And we are looking forward, not backwards. 

MODERATOR:  Next we’ll go to Andres Magnusson from the Icelandic Morgunbladid.

QUESTION:  Yeah.  And Mr. Secretary, I’m also asking on behalf of Visir.  But this summer, the U.S. asked Iceland, sent actually a questionnaire, about support for U.S. foreign policy priorities.  How do you view the Iceland response?  And also, in light of how warmly you speak of Icelandic-U.S. relations, where do you think there is space to deepen the relationship?  Where could it be strengthened?  And if I might add, is the U.S. willing to explore a free trade agreement with Iceland? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, a couple points.  On – about questionnaires and things like that, we’re always probing to see where we stand in comparison to what our priorities are and where that is of other countries.  You’re never going to have a hundred percent on every issue, but that’s okay.  But I would say our alignment with Iceland is generally very concrete.  I mean, I think we share the same perspectives of the world.  I think we share a lot in common.  We have a shared history, which brings us to the conclusion that we identify the same things as threats and the same things as opportunities.  And so that’s the way that I view that.

And so in the context of that – what was the second part of your question?  Because I need to start writing these things down.  These guys come with three-part questions.  And – go ahead, I’m sorry. 

QUESTION:  Well, the second part was about – you spoke warmly of (inaudible), where do you think —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, places to grow.  Yeah, so I think —

QUESTION:  Yeah.  And the free trade agreement.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, look – and the free trade agreement.  That one I wrote.  That one I did write down.

So on places where we can grow, I think I’ve highlighted some of those for you already today.  Look, security is always important, right?  Security underpins everything else.  If you’re not secure, you can’t be prosperous.  So I think there’s no doubt that – but we’re not starting from zero here.  We have a history of security cooperation.  What has changed is the world and the threats.  What the threats looked like 20 years ago, 30 years ago are different than what they would look like today, so we have to modernize. 

But we already have a baseline and a foundation of cooperation that extends all the way back for 75 years, so we’re not building something new here.  We’re simply modernizing it.  So there’s no doubt that on the security realm there’s very – ability to cooperate and continue to cooperate, and not just with the United States but with all of our NATO Allies, particularly those in the High North and that are involved in Arctic defense.

And – but beyond that, I think the economic opportunities are very real.  You have very unique companies here that do some very unique things in the pharmaceutical realm, in biotechnology, in a variety of fields that we think there are real opportunities for them to do business in the United States.  And likewise, I think there are some business opportunities potentially here that we’d like to present to American investors, which is why what we’d like to do as a follow-up, as a concrete follow-up to my visit here, is organize visits of American businesses here to identify those opportunities and see if there’s some synergy, and likewise invite companies from Iceland to come to the United States and find sectors and areas where they could also invest in our economy or find markets.  So I think that’s very positive.

As far as free trade agreements are concerned, look, I think the era of free trade agreements for the foreseeable future is probably not going to be there.  I mean not with Iceland but just in general writ large.  Where I do think we have real opportunities is a bilateral trade agreement – bilateral trade, a reciprocal trade understanding between our countries.  And it’s my understanding that meetings to try to pursue and further that are being organized as already pre-existing to my visit, and hopefully those will be very positive.

And that ties in perfectly to my previous answer to you, which is there are companies here to do very unique things that we would like to see in the United States, and there are companies in the United States that I think could find some real positive economic opportunities to invest and be a part of here.  And we just want to – we want to use the government, our embassy, our presence here, your embassy in the United States, to connect and create that synergy.  And we will both benefit from it.  You’ll become more prosperous, we’ll become more prosperous, and I think it will only bind us together more closely. 

MODERATOR:  Thank you.  And lastly we will go to Shannon Kingston from ABC News.

QUESTION:  Thank you very much, Mr. Secretary, Madam Foreign Minister.  A question on – the State Department has assessed that Russia maintains an active offensive bioweapons program.  There are also reports now that the FSB is involved in a forceful response to the recent fatal suspected plague death in Siberia.  My question for you is – for you both is:  Do you see any reason to suspect that what we’re seeing now might be the accidental release of an intentionally modified strain of the plague that was altered by Russia?  What is your level of concern?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well look, first of all, anytime you hear that there is some disease that infected someone in a lab anywhere in the world, you’re going to be concerned about it, especially given recent events not so long ago, obviously, in 2021 and 2020 when we saw that happen. 

That said, it would be irresponsible for me here to sit and speculate because we just don’t have all the information yet.  I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world.  That’s what they should do.  That’s what we hope they will do.  And the more we can learn about what happened, then the better all of us can be in a position of responding.  And maybe there’s nothing there.  Maybe it’s bigger than we thought.  We don’t know. 

But I think it would be reckless at this moment given the limited information we still have to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn’t.  Suffice it to say we’re watching it very closely, and I think the whole world is watching it very closely, because depending on what we learn about it, we would know how to respond.  We already have measures in place to be able to address it if it’s something more serious than what so far has been acknowledged. 

Suffice it to say we’re glad to be aware of it.  We’re watching it very closely hour by hour.  We have multiple agencies not just in the United States but internationally that are watching it.  We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately, but we’ll have to make those decisions on the basis of the information that we’re learning and are being provided.  And so far that’s still quite limited, but hopefully that will change in the next few hours and days.

MODERATOR:  And with that we conclude this press conference.  Thank you very much.

FOREIGN MINISTER GUNNARSDÓTTIR:  Thank you. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.
